title: Time to peace
hook: Berakhot begins with a question about time and ends with peace
tomorrow: the last page is done. so is the book finished, or just begun?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hadran, the goodbye said to a finished book: we will return to you. So let's return now, all the way to page one.
screen: `WE WILL RETURN TO YOU.` → `BACK TO PAGE ONE.`

segments.voice: Look at the alarms on a phone. Six-forty. Six-forty-five. Six-fifty. A whole life can feel like it's run by a clock. Berakhot opens with one. Its very first word is a question, me'eimatai: from when? From when do we say the Shema in the evening? And its last word, as you heard, is peace. A book that starts with a clock and ends with peace. Why?
screen: `SIX-FORTY. SIX-FORTY-FIVE.` → `FIRST WORD: FROM WHEN?` → `LAST WORD: PEACE.`

segments.voice: Start with page one, in plain words. The Mishnah asks from when the evening Shema can be said, and answers: from nightfall. Then the sages argue about until when. Some say midnight. Rabban Gamliel says until dawn. And here's something to tell a friend tonight: his sons come home late from a party and ask, is it too late to say the Shema? He tells them: if dawn hasn't come, you still can. The very first page of the book of blessings has kids home late, asking if they missed it. Second puzzle: why does it start with evening, not morning? The Talmud asks that itself. One answer is the Shema's own verse, "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up": lying down comes first. Another is creation: "And there was evening and there was morning, one day." In Jewish time, the day begins in the dark. Now the big puzzle. One way some readers put it together: the tractate begins with when do I owe this, and ends with what is it all for. It starts with obligation counted in hours, and after all those blessings, over bread, scent, places, waking, loss, it arrives at peace. The clock doesn't disappear. It turns out to be the road. Small, timed acts of blessing are how a person gets from time to peace.
screen: `FROM WHEN? FROM NIGHTFALL.` · `TOO LATE? NOT IF DAWN HASN'T COME.` · `EVENING FIRST, LIKE CREATION.` · `THE CLOCK IS THE ROAD.` · then, large: `FROM TIME TO PEACE.`

segments.voice: Count three things on your fingers: three lines from these weeks of Berakhot you'd want to keep. Say each one quietly as you count it, and notice which one surprised you most. If a fourth comes, let it.
Time to peace. The shape of the whole tractate: it opens asking from when, and closes with peace.
Your line: from time to peace, and the clock is the road. That's forty-eight of fifty.

screen: `DAY 1535 COUNTS.` → `BERAKHOT · 48 OF 50.` → `TOMORROW: THE LAST PAGE IS DONE. SO IS THE BOOK FINISHED, OR JUST BEGUN?`

howItsDone: At a siyum, learners often look back over the whole tractate, from its opening question to its last line; the Jewish day, and the evening Shema, begin at nightfall.

chat.meaning: Berakhot opens with a clock, from when, and closes with peace. The middle, all those small timed blessings, is the road between them.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 (recipe v3): puzzle shape. The odd detail: a book of blessings opens with a clock. The solution ('from when do I owe this' to 'what it is for') is voiced as 'one way some readers put it together'; it's an interpretive frame, not a claim of the text.

Mishnah Berakhot 1:1 paraphrased: 'from nightfall' simplifies 'from the time the priests enter to eat their terumah'; 'some say midnight' simplifies Rabbi Eliezer (end of the first watch) and the Sages (midnight). Confirm the simplification.
Rabban Gamliel's sons 'come home late from a party' renders 'came from a banquet hall / wedding feast'; confirm.
Deuteronomy 6:7 and Genesis 1:5 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm exact wording.
